topics.title: Naming Organic Compounds
topics.notesHtml:
Naming Organic Compounds

The names of organic compounds can be split into 2 parts:

  1. Prefix shows the number of carbon atoms in one molecule
  2. Suffix shows the homologous series the compound belongs to
Number of Carbon atomsPrefix
1Meth-
2Eth-
3Prop-
4But-
5Pent-
6Hex-
7Hept-
8Oct-
9Non-
10Dec-
SuffixHomologous Series
-aneAlkane
-eneAlkene
-olAlcohol
-oic acidCarboxylic Acid

Note: Since alkenes consist of a C=C double bond, there is no such thing as "methene".

Branched Carbon Chains

For non-straight carbon chains, the alkyl group will appear in the name. For example, 2-methylpropane is an isomer of butane.

The carbon chain should be rearranged such that branches form out of the longest possible chain. For example, a compound that at first glance may seem to be "2-ethylpropane" is actually wrong: when rewritten with the longest carbon chain, it becomes a 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon, i.e. 2-methylbutane.

Functional Groups and Isomer Naming

For certain homologous series, the placement of the functional group produces different compounds with the same molecular formula (isomers). This applies to alcohols as well as alkenes, where the number represents the carbon atom which the double bond starts from (e.g. but-1-ene has its double bond at the end while but-2-ene has it in the centre).

Addition of Halogens

With the addition/substitution of halogens, the name of the resultant compound will start with the position of the halogen atoms in relation to the carbon atoms, followed by the prefix (di, tri, tetra, etc.) chloro/bromo/fluoro and the alkane name.

For the combination of the above naming rules, the halogen is named first, followed by the alkyl branch and the functional group, e.g. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

Isomers: Compounds which share the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Isomers have different physical properties (e.g. melting point, boiling point) but chemically behave in the same way.

topics.title: Alkanes
topics.notesHtml:
Alkanes

Alkanes: Hydrocarbons that contain only carbon-carbon single covalent bonds (saturated hydrocarbons).

General Formula: CnH2n+2. Each member of the alkane family differs from the next by a -CH2- unit.

Number of C atomsAlkaneMolecular Formula
1MethaneCH4
2EthaneC2H6
3PropaneC3H8
4ButaneC4H10

Isomerism in Alkanes

From butane onwards, other than the typical straight carbon chains, alkanes can also form isomers with alkyl groups.

Alkyl groups have the general formula CnH2n+1 and include: Methyl (CH3-), Ethyl (CH3CH2-), Propyl (CH3CH2CH2-), Butyl (CH3CH2CH2CH2-).

Take butane (C4H10) as an example: other than the 4-carbon straight chain, it can form a 3-carbon chain with a methyl branch from the central carbon (2-methylpropane).

Pentane (C5H12) has 3 isomers:

  • Pentane, C5H12 – 5-carbon chain (longest)
  • 2-methylbutane – 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon atom
  • 2,2-dimethylpropane – 3-carbon chain with 2 methyl groups attached to the 2nd carbon atom

To find isomers, systematically remove a CH3 group (methyl group) from the end of the chain and see where else it can fit in place of one of the other hydrogens (the hydrogen joins the carbon atom that the methyl group came from).

Note: It may seem possible to form another isomer using an ethyl group on a 3-carbon chain, but as stated before, the longest chain must be used – this is actually a 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon, i.e. 2-methylbutane. When working with structural isomers, always ensure the longest chain is drawn horizontal.

Physical Properties of Alkanes

  • Low melting point (MPT) and boiling point (BPT); the first 4 members in the series exist as gases at room temperature and pressure (rtp)
  • Insoluble in water
  • Soluble in organic solvents

Down the series: molecular size increases, intermolecular forces of attraction (IMFOA) between alkane molecules increase, and more energy is required to overcome the IMFOA between molecules. Thus, down the series:

  1. MPT and BPT of alkanes increase
  2. Alkanes become more viscous (flow less easily)
  3. Flammability decreases – percentage of carbon increases, making the alkane harder to burn and producing a smokier flame

Chemical Properties of Alkanes

1. Combustion

Alkanes burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce CO2 and H2O vapour. If oxygen is limited, H2O will still form along with CO and C (as soot). CO is odourless, colourless and poisonous, hence dangerous, as it interferes with the way oxygen is carried around the body. The reaction is highly exothermic (produces a lot of heat), hence alkanes are used as fuels.

  • Complete: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(l) + heat energy
  • Incomplete: 4CH4(g) + 5O2(g) → 2CO(g) + 8H2O(l) + 2C(s) + heat energy

2. Substitution Reaction

Substitution reactions occur when an atom in a molecule is replaced by a different atom. Alkanes react with halogens (Cl2, Br2, etc.) in the presence of UV light, which triggers the reaction by splitting the Cl2 or Br2 molecules into individual atoms.

For the reaction between methane and chlorine gas, a colourless gas, chloromethane (CH3Cl), is produced along with fumes of HCl gas. A similar reaction occurs with Br2 instead of Cl2, producing bromomethane and hydrogen bromide.

With successive reactions, more hydrogen atoms in the alkane are replaced by chlorine atoms, until all hydrogen atoms are substituted. Note that the reaction cannot result in H2 gas produced and 2 chlorine atoms substituted into the alkane in one step – dichloroalkanes form via successive reactions.

For reactions involving larger alkanes, the placement of halogen atoms may affect the product achieved. With propane, the hydrogen replaced could be at either the middle or end of the chain, so 2 different molecules may be formed from the substitution of chlorine:

  • 1-chloropropane: CH3CH2CH2Cl
  • 2-chloropropane: CH3CHClCH3

topics.title: Alkenes
topics.notesHtml:
Alkenes

Alkenes: Hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds (unsaturated hydrocarbons).

General Formula: CnH2n. Each member of the alkene family differs from the next by a -CH2- unit. Functional group: C=C.

Number of C atomsAlkeneMolecular Formula
2EtheneC2H4
3PropeneC3H6
4ButeneC4H8

Isomerism in Alkenes

Similar to alkanes, from butene onwards, alkenes can form isomers with alkyl groups. As seen from the naming of organic compounds, alkenes also form isomers depending on where the functional group (C=C bond) starts. Butene, C4H8, has 3 isomers.

Physical Properties of Alkenes

Physical properties of alkenes are similar to those of alkanes:

  • Low MPT and BPT (the first 3 in the series exist as gases at rtp)
  • Insoluble in water
  • Soluble in organic solvents

Down the series: molecular size increases, IMFOA between alkene molecules increases, and more energy is required to overcome the IMFOA between molecules. Thus, down the series: MPT and BPT increase, alkenes become more viscous (flow less easily), and flammability decreases as percentage of carbon increases (harder to burn, smokier flame produced).

Chemical Properties of Alkenes

1. Combustion

Alkenes burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce CO2 and H2O vapour. As alkenes contain a higher percentage of carbon (being unsaturated) than the corresponding alkanes, incomplete combustion is more likely. Hence they burn with a sootier flame (carbon is 81.8% of propane but 85.7% of propene).

C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(g) (with heat)

2. Addition Reaction

The carbon-carbon double bonds (C=C) in alkenes are very reactive. Due to the property of its functional group, alkenes readily undergo addition reactions, in which an unsaturated organic compound combines with another substance to form a new single compound.

  • a. Hydrogenation: Addition of H2 to alkenes to form alkanes. Conditions: 200°C, nickel catalyst. Note: this reaction may seem pointless as ethene is a very useful compound used to make many things, while ethane is only a fuel.
  • b. Bromination: Addition of Br2 to alkenes. This reaction is used to test for the presence of unsaturated hydrocarbons and can be used to distinguish between an alkane and an alkene. Bromine water is used instead of the dangerous liquid bromine.
    AlkaneAlkene
    Ethane does not decolourise bromine solution under normal conditions. Bromine remains reddish-brown.Ethene decolourises the solution. Bromine solution turns from reddish-brown to colourless.
  • c. Hydration: Addition of steam (H2O) to alkenes to form alcohols. Conditions: 300°C, 60 atm, phosphoric(V) acid catalyst (H3PO4).

3. Addition Polymerisation

Reaction between alkene molecules (monomers) to form a long molecule (polymer). Conditions: high temperature and pressure, catalyst. (More on polymerisation is covered under macromolecules.)

Production of Alkenes

Cracking: Breaking down of long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons or hydrogen.

Alkenes are obtained by cracking petroleum. For example, nonane can be broken down to form heptane and ethene: C9H20 → C7H16 + C2H4.

Breaking the long hydrocarbon chain produces 2 fragments, but these fragments are not viable on their own and need some rearrangement of hydrogen atoms – a hydrogen atom from the far-right CH3 is transferred to the CH2 on the left-hand fragment.

The nonane molecule can also break at different points to produce other fragments, e.g. C9H20 → C6H14 + C3H6.

Industrial Catalytic CrackingCracking in the School Lab
In catalytic cracking, a catalyst is used to speed up the process of cracking. Conditions: high temperature (e.g. 600°C), aluminium oxide (Al2O3) and silicon dioxide (SiO2) catalysts.

Importance of Cracking

  1. Production of short-chain alkenes, e.g. C18H38 → C6H14 + 6C2H4. Short-chain alkenes like ethene and propene are extremely useful and can be used to make ethanol and plastics.
  2. Production of hydrogen, e.g. C18H38 → C8H16 + C10H20 + H2. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of ammonia, which is used to make fertilisers.
  3. Converting hydrocarbons of higher molecular mass into smaller molecules which are in higher demand – for example, there is a higher demand for petrol than lubricating oil or diesel oil. Petrol can be obtained through catalytic cracking of diesel and lubricating oils.

Alkanes vs Alkenes

Both are hydrocarbons; both are flammable and burn completely in excess oxygen to produce CO2 and H2O.

AlkanesAlkenes
Contain only C-C (single) bondsContain one or more C=C (double) bonds
Generally unreactiveVery reactive
Undergo substitution reactions; do not react with aqueous bromine under normal conditions (requires UV light and time)Undergo addition reactions; rapidly decolourise aqueous bromine
Produce a less smoky flame than an alkene with the same number of carbon atomsProduce a smokier flame than an alkane with the same number of carbon atoms
Do not undergo polymerisationUndergo addition polymerisation

topics.title: Alcohols
topics.notesHtml:
Alcohols

Alcohols: Series of organic compounds which have the hydroxyl (-OH) functional group.

General Formula: CnH2n+1OH. Functional group: -OH.

Number of C atomsAlcoholMolecular Formula
1MethanolCH3OH
2EthanolC2H5OH
3PropanolC3H7OH
4ButanolC4H9OH

Physical Properties of Alcohols

Alcohols are volatile liquids at rtp. Down the series: molecular size increases, IMFOA increases, solubility of alcohols decreases, and BPT of alcohols increases.

AlcoholPhysical StateSolubility in WaterBoiling Point (°C)
MethanolLiquidVery Soluble65
EthanolLiquidVery Soluble78
PropanolLiquidSoluble97
ButanolLiquidSlightly Soluble118

Chemical Properties of Alcohols

1. Combustion

Alcohols burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce carbon dioxide and water vapour: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O. This reaction is highly exothermic (produces a lot of heat), hence alcohols are used as fuels.

2. Oxidation

Alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids when heated with oxidising agents such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4 (or potassium dichromate(VI), K2Cr2O7).

Conditions: excess of oxidising agent; heat the mixture for a long time.

If KMnO4 is used as the oxidising agent, the colour of the solution will change from purple to colourless (note: if KMnO4 is added in excess, the colour will not turn colourless but instead remain a light purple).

Breathalysers

The police use breathalysers to test the amount of alcohol consumed by drivers. It contains an oxidising agent, usually acidified potassium dichromate, and a catalyst. A colour change is registered if a certain amount of alcohol is present in the breath.

Production of Ethanol

1. Catalytic Addition of Steam to Ethene

Conditions: 300°C, 60 atm, phosphoric(V) acid catalyst (H3PO4).

2. Fermentation of Carbohydrates

Alcohol fermentation occurs when a microorganism such as yeast acts on carbohydrates (glucose, fructose, sucrose) in anaerobic conditions (absence of oxygen) to produce ethanol and CO2.

In the laboratory, glucose solution is mixed with yeast and kept at 37°C. Carbon dioxide produced during fermentation forms a white precipitate in limewater.

A dilute solution of ethanol (15% alcohol) is produced. A higher alcohol content is not produced as it causes the yeast to die and fermentation to stop. Ethanol can be extracted by fractional distillation. This allows for higher concentrations of alcoholic beverages or pure ethanol to be produced.

Precautions:

  • Fermentation only takes place in anaerobic conditions, hence the flask must be tightly stoppered.
  • Limewater is used as an air lock.
  • Temperature should be kept at 37°C or the enzymes will be denatured and fermentation will stop.

When wine or beer is left exposed to air in the open for a few days, it turns sour. Ethanol undergoes oxidation to form ethanoic acid (vinegar); thus fermentation of carbohydrates only takes place in the absence of oxygen.

Uses of Ethanol

  • In alcoholic drinks (beer, wine, rum, sake)

  • As a fuel in cars (often mixed with petrol)

topics.title: Carboxylic Acids
topics.notesHtml:
Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic Acids: Series of organic acids which have the carboxyl (-COOH) functional group.

General Formula: CnH2n+1COOH (note: since the functional group already contains a C, methanoic acid starts from n=0). Functional group: -COOH.

Number of C atomsCarboxylic AcidFormula
1Methanoic AcidHCOOH
2Ethanoic AcidCH3COOH
3Propanoic AcidC2H5COOH
4Butanoic AcidC3H7COOH

Physical Properties of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are very soluble in water and exist as colourless liquids at rtp. Their boiling points are above that of water and increase down the series (with increasing molecular size).

Carboxylic acids are weak acids as they ionise partially in water, i.e. low concentration of H+ ions (pH 5-6). Due to the hydrogen ions produced, carboxylic acids have acidic properties.

The CH3COO- ions are called ethanoate ions. Due to the structure of ethanoate (or any other ion from a carboxylic acid), cations are attracted to the O- in the anion. Hence salts formed are written as, e.g., (CH3COO)2Mg – this keeps the structure of the compound more understandable, instead of writing Mg(OOCCH3)2.

Chemical Properties of Carboxylic Acids

1. Simple Acid Reactions

  • a. Reaction with Reactive Metals: Like all acids, metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series will react with carboxylic acids. Carboxylic Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen. E.g. 2CH3COOH(aq) + Mg(s) → (CH3COO)2Mg(aq) + H2(g)
  • b. Reaction with Carbonates: carboxylic acid + carbonate → salt + carbon dioxide + water
  • c. Reaction with Bases: carboxylic acid + base → salt + water
  • d. Esterification: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols under certain conditions to produce a new compound called an ester. carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water

Production of Ethanoic Acid

1. Oxidation of Ethanol with Acidified KMnO4

Potassium manganate(VII) acts as an oxidising agent and is reduced. Its colour changes from purple to colourless. Since ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, ethanol acts as a reducing agent.

2. Oxidation of Ethanol by Atmospheric Oxygen

Certain bacteria in the air oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid. Thus, alcoholic drinks turn sour when left exposed to air for a few days.

topics.title: Esters
topics.notesHtml:
Esters

Esters: An organic compound derived from carboxylic acids with the -COO- functional group.

  • Sweet-smelling, colourless liquids that are insoluble in water
  • Contain the -COO- functional group
  • Formed by the reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, also known as esterification

Esterification

Conditions: warmed, with a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 as catalyst.

  • A warm water bath is used instead of a direct flame, as all the organic components of the mixture are flammable; ethyl ethanoate also has a low boiling point.
  • The ester is poured into cold water after the reaction, as everything else in the mixture dissolves in water, leaving the insoluble ester layer which can be smelt (this gets rid of the strong smell of the ethanoic acid).

For example, ethanoic acid and ethanol react in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form water and an ester called ethyl ethanoate. The -OH in ethanoic acid is replaced by the -C2H5O from ethanol, and joins the remaining H to form water.

Naming Esters

The name of an ester consists of 2 parts: the first part is derived from the alcohol, and the second part is derived from the carboxylic acid.

Uses of Esters

  • In the preparation of perfumes
  • As artificial food flavourings
  • As solvents for cosmetics and glues
  • In soaps – naturally-occurring esters such as animal fats and vegetable oils are boiled with sodium hydroxide to form soap

topics.title: Macromolecules and Polymerisation
topics.notesHtml:
Macromolecules

Macromolecule: A very large molecule made up of many small molecules.

A polymer is a type of long-chain macromolecule that is covalently linked together by many small repeat units called monomers. Different polymers are made up of different monomers.

Natural PolymersSynthetic Polymers
Proteins, DNA, Starch, Cellulose, Wool, Natural rubber, SilkPoly(ethene), Nylon, Terylene, Polyvinyl chloride (PVC), Polyvinyl acetate (PVA), Teflon, Polystyrene

Polymerisation: Process of joining together a large number of monomers to form a polymer. There are 2 types of polymerisation: Addition Polymerisation and Condensation Polymerisation.

Addition Polymerisation

Addition Polymerisation: When monomer units join together without losing any molecules or atoms.

Alkenes have reactive C=C bonds, hence can undergo addition polymerisation.

Conditions (not definite; differs based on type of polymer and polymer length): high pressure (e.g. 1000 atm), high temperature (e.g. 200°C), catalyst.

Example: Ethene → Poly(ethene). The formula of the polymer can be written using its repeat unit. The letter 'n' represents a large number of repeat units. The number of ethene molecules in each poly(ethene) molecule varies between 10,000 and 30,000.

Deducing the Structural Formula of a Polymer/Monomer

  1. Given a monomer, e.g. propene, C3H6, and asked to draw a length of poly(propene) chain: draw the given monomer such that all the attachments are kept out of the way of the C=C bond, then derive the repeat unit by splitting the double bond, then draw the required length of chain, ensuring extension bonds are included to show that the polymer extends beyond the drawn chain.
  2. Given a polymer, e.g. PVA (polyvinyl acetate), and asked to draw the structural formula of the monomer: identify and write down the formula of the repeat unit, then convert the C-C single bond into a C=C double bond, giving the structural formula of the monomer.

Uses of Addition Polymers

Addition polymers are good insulators of heat and electricity, and are resistant to chemical attack.

  • Poly(ethene) can be easily moulded into different shapes. It is used to make plastic toys, clingfilm, plastic bags, and buckets.
  • Polystyrene is hard, light and brittle. It is used to make disposable containers.
  • Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is used to make pipes, raincoats, flooring mats and thin gloves.
  • Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) is used in 'non-stick' frying pans.
  • Perspex is used for the windscreens of cars.

Condensation Polymerisation

Condensation Polymerisation: When monomer units join together to form a polymer with the loss/removal of a small molecule (e.g. water).

Condensation polymers are made from two different monomers with a functional group at each end of each monomer, thus giving the polymer a linkage of its own. This linkage depends on the type of condensation polymer. There are two types of condensation polymers: polyamides and polyesters.

Polyamides

The monomers of polyamides (e.g. Nylon) are a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine.

  • Dicarboxylic acid: any acid with a carboxyl (-COOH) functional group at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).
  • Diamine: any amine with an amine functional group (-NH2) at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).

When a dicarboxylic acid is reacted with a diamine, the breaking of C-O bonds and N-H bonds occurs to form water, which is removed. The repeat unit of a polyamide contains the amide linkage (-CONH-), as suggested by the name "polyamide".

Polyesters

The monomers of polyesters (e.g. Terylene) are a dicarboxylic acid and a diol.

  • Dicarboxylic acid: any acid with a carboxyl (-COOH) functional group at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).
  • Diol: any alcohol with a hydroxyl functional group (-OH) at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).

When a dicarboxylic acid is reacted with a diol, the breaking of C-O bonds and O-H bonds occurs to form water, which is removed. The repeat unit of a polyester contains the ester linkage (-COO-), as suggested by the name "polyester".

Uses of Man-made Fibres

  • Synthetic or man-made fibres are usually plastics which have been spun into threads.
  • Terylene and nylon are the best-known examples of synthetic fibres.
  • Clothes made from these fibres are shrink-proof and crease-proof. They are also easier to wash and dry.
  • Examples of items made from nylon and Terylene include curtains, parachutes, fishing lines and sleeping bags.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Plastics

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Easily moulded into various shapes; Light, tough and waterproof; Durable (note: do not say "cheap" or "relatively cheap")Land Pollution: Plastics are non-biodegradable (do not break down and decompose easily) and are not decomposed by bacteria in the soil, leading to a build-up of waste.
Air Pollution: Plastics are flammable. When plastics burn, fires can spread very quickly and poisonous gases are produced.
Water Pollution: Plastics thrown into the sea endanger marine animals, which mistake plastics for food and choke on them. Plastics can also clog up rivers and drains, which may become breeding grounds for mosquitoes.

flashcards.q: What is a polymer?
flashcards.a: A type of long-chain macromolecule that is covalently linked together by many small repeat units called monomers.

flashcards.q: Give three examples of natural polymers.
flashcards.a: Proteins, DNA, starch (also cellulose, wool, natural rubber, silk).

flashcards.q: Give three examples of synthetic polymers.
flashcards.a: Poly(ethene), Nylon, Terylene (also PVC, PVA, Teflon, polystyrene).

flashcards.q: What is polymerisation?
flashcards.a: The process of joining together a large number of monomers to form a polymer.

flashcards.q: What are the two types of polymerisation?
flashcards.a: Addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.

flashcards.q: What is addition polymerisation?
flashcards.a: When monomer units join together without losing any molecules or atoms.

flashcards.q: What is condensation polymerisation?
flashcards.a: When monomer units join together to form a polymer with the loss/removal of a small molecule (e.g. water).

flashcards.q: What monomers form polyamides like Nylon?
flashcards.a: A dicarboxylic acid and a diamine.

flashcards.q: What monomers form polyesters like Terylene?
flashcards.a: A dicarboxylic acid and a diol.

flashcards.q: What linkage is found in polyamides?
flashcards.a: The amide linkage (-CONH-).

flashcards.q: What linkage is found in polyesters?
flashcards.a: The ester linkage (-COO-).

flashcards.q: What small molecule is lost during formation of polyamides and polyesters?
flashcards.a: Water.

flashcards.q: Give two uses of poly(ethene).
flashcards.a: Plastic toys, clingfilm (also plastic bags, buckets).

flashcards.q: What is a key disadvantage of plastics regarding land pollution?
flashcards.a: Plastics are non-biodegradable and are not decomposed by bacteria in soil, leading to waste build-up.

flashcards.q: What is Teflon used for?
flashcards.a: Non-stick frying pans.

quiz.question: What is a polymer?
choices: A long-chain macromolecule made of repeat units called monomers
quiz.explanation: A polymer is a long-chain macromolecule covalently linked by repeating monomer units.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
quiz.explanation: Starch is listed as a natural polymer, while Nylon, Terylene, and PVC are synthetic.

quiz.question: What distinguishes condensation polymerisation from addition polymerisation?
choices: Addition polymerisation loses water; condensation does not
Condensation polymerisation loses a small molecule like water; addition does not
quiz.explanation: Condensation polymerisation involves loss of a small molecule (e.g. water), unlike addition polymerisation.

quiz.question: What monomers combine to form a polyamide like Nylon?
choices: A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
quiz.explanation: Polyamides form from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, joined via amide linkages.

quiz.question: What linkage characterises a polyester such as Terylene?
quiz.explanation: Polyesters like Terylene contain the ester linkage (-COO-) formed from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol.

quiz.question: Why are plastics considered a land pollution problem?
choices: They are non-biodegradable and not decomposed by soil bacteria
They are heavier than other waste
quiz.explanation: Plastics are non-biodegradable, so they build up in the environment instead of decomposing.

quiz.question: What conditions are typically needed for addition polymerisation of alkenes?
choices: Low pressure, low temperature, no catalyst
quiz.explanation: Addition polymerisation of alkenes typically requires high pressure, high temperature and a catalyst.

quiz.question: How many types of condensation polymers are described in the notes?
choices: Four — including nylon, Terylene, PVC, and PVA
quiz.explanation: The notes state there are two types of condensation polymers: polyamides (like Nylon) and polyesters (like Terylene).

quiz.question: Based on the general properties of addition polymers described in the notes, why is Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) suitable for making non-stick frying pans?
choices: Addition polymers are resistant to chemical attack, so Teflon does not react with food during cooking
Addition polymers are formed through condensation reactions, releasing water that prevents sticking
Addition polymers are biodegradable, so Teflon breaks down safely after use
Addition polymers conduct heat and electricity well, allowing even cooking
quiz.explanation: The notes state that addition polymers are resistant to chemical attack (and good insulators), which explains why Teflon is used for non-stick pans — it doesn't react with the food being cooked.

quiz.question: A company wants to make curtains and sleeping bags that are shrink-proof and crease-proof, and easier to wash and dry than natural fibres. Which polymers, per the notes, would be suitable?
quiz.explanation: The notes identify Terylene and nylon as the best-known synthetic fibres, describing items (such as curtains and sleeping bags) made from them as shrink-proof, crease-proof, and easier to wash and dry.

quiz.question: A condensation polymer's repeat unit is found to contain the amide linkage -CONH-. Based on the notes, what two types of monomers, with what functional groups, must have combined to form this polymer?
choices: A dicarboxylic acid (-COOH at both ends) and a diol (-OH at both ends)
A dicarboxylic acid (-COOH at both ends) and a diamine (-NH2 at both ends)
A diamine (-NH2 at both ends) and a diol (-OH at both ends)
An alkene monomer containing a C=C bond at each end
quiz.explanation: The notes state that polyamides such as Nylon are formed from a dicarboxylic acid (-COOH at both ends) and a diamine (-NH2 at both ends), and that the repeat unit of a polyamide contains the amide linkage -CONH-.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the notes as a form of pollution caused by plastics?
choices: Ozone layer depletion caused by gases released from plastics
Land pollution, since plastics are non-biodegradable and build up in soil
Air pollution, since burning plastics produces poisonous gases
Water pollution, since marine animals mistake plastics for food and choke on them
quiz.explanation: The notes describe land, air, and water pollution caused by plastics, but do not mention ozone layer depletion as one of the pollution problems associated with plastics.

Condensation polymerisation occurs when monomer units join together with the loss of a small molecule such as water, e.g. a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine forming Nylon (a polyamide) with loss of water.

shortAnswer.prompt: Discuss the environmental disadvantages of plastics, covering land, air and water pollution.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Plastics cause land pollution because they are non-biodegradable and are not decomposed by bacteria in soil, leading to a build-up of waste. They cause air pollution because they are flammable; when burned, fires can spread quickly and produce poisonous gases. They cause water pollution because plastics thrown into the sea endanger marine animals, which may mistake them for food and choke, and they can clog rivers and drains, creating mosquito breeding grounds.
